title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (InstructGPT)
authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, Diogo Almeida, Carroll L. Wainwright, Pamela Mishkin, Chong Zhang, Sandhini Agarwal, Katarina Slama, Alex Ray, et al.

pages.title: Aligning LLMs to human intent with RLHF

blocks.html: GPT-3 was extraordinarily capable but frequently unhelpful in practice — it might invent plausible-sounding answers, refuse to follow a stated style, or output harmful content. The base objective (predict the next token of internet text) doesn't optimize for 'be useful to the person asking.'
InstructGPT is the recipe that turned GPT-3 into something usable as a chat assistant. Three stages, applied on top of a pre-trained base model:

items: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human-written demonstrations of helpful responses.
Reward model (RM) trained on human preference comparisons between pairs of model outputs.
Reinforcement learning using PPO against the reward model to fine-tune the SFT model.

blocks.html: Result: a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model is preferred to the 175B GPT-3 by human labelers in 85% of comparisons. Alignment beats scale, by a lot.

Collect ~13,000 prompts (sampled from the OpenAI API user submissions, plus labeler-written prompts). For each prompt, a human contractor writes a demonstration of the desired output. Fine-tune the base GPT-3 on these (prompt → demonstration) pairs with standard supervised learning.

This already produces a much more usable model than the base — but it's bottlenecked on how much demonstration data you can collect (expensive), and demonstrations only capture one possible good answer per prompt.
Sample multiple completions from the SFT model for each of ~33,000 prompts. Human labelers rank the completions from best to worst.
Train a separate reward model (initialized from a smaller pre-trained LM, 6B parameters in the paper) on these pairwise comparisons. The loss is the Bradley-Terry pairwise ranking loss:
where $y_w$ is the preferred (winning) completion and $y_l$ is the rejected (losing) one. The reward model learns to assign higher scalar scores to responses humans prefer.
Comparisons are dramatically cheaper to collect than demonstrations and yield much higher-quality signal because they capture relative preferences across many possible answers.
Now fine-tune the SFT model using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), treating the reward model's score as the reward. At each step:

items: Sample a prompt $x$ and generate a completion $y$ from the policy $\pi$.

Add a per-token KL penalty against the SFT policy: $r' = r - \beta \log(\pi(y|x) / \pi_{\text{SFT}}(y|x))$. This keeps the RL-tuned model close to the SFT model so it doesn't drift into adversarial regions that exploit the reward model.

blocks.html: Optionally, mix in a small amount of the original pre-training loss (PPO-ptx variant) to retain core LM capabilities.

pages.title: Human preference: InstructGPT beats GPT-3 at much smaller scale

blocks.html: Headline finding: InstructGPT 1.3B is preferred to GPT-3 175B in 85% of head-to-head comparisons by labelers, even though it has 100× fewer parameters.

items: More truthful: 2× as likely to be truthful as GPT-3 on TruthfulQA.
Less toxic: ~25% reduction in toxic generations on RealToxicityPrompts.
Better instruction following: stronger compliance with explicit constraints (length, style, format).

blocks.html: Tradeoff: small alignment tax on academic NLP benchmarks (the model loses ~1-2 points on things like SQuAD because it's optimized for instruction following, not benchmark-style completion). The PPO-ptx variant mitigates this.

pages.title: Why RLHF is now the default

blocks.html: InstructGPT is the technical foundation under ChatGPT (released Nov 2022, applying the same recipe to a tuned GPT-3.5). Every major frontier chat model since uses some variant of RLHF (or its modern descendants — DPO, RLAIF, Constitutional AI).

Bigger picture: this paper shifted the field's attention from capability to alignment. The pre-trained base is the substrate; the human-feedback loop is what makes it useful and safe. Modern post-training pipelines spend an order of magnitude more effort here than was customary before this paper.
